title: Seeing Structure, Reading Blood
endLine: MRI maps structure; fMRI reads blood oxygenation, not spikes or cause.

scenes.tts: How can you map a living human brain without opening the skull? Magnetic resonance imaging, or M R I, pictures brain structure. Functional M R I adds glowing patches during a task. What do those glowing patches measure?
scenes.caption: How can you map a living human brain without opening the skull? Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, pictures brain structure. Functional MRI adds glowing patches during a task. What do those glowing patches measure?
scenes.visual: One carried world fills at least 60% of frame height: a schematic human brain resting inside a clean MRI scanner ring on a dark slate background. First, crisp gray and white structural outlines sweep across the brain slice. Next, a warm glowing patch blooms across cortex as a bold high-contrast question mark appears beside it; the scanner ring's subtle magnetic field lines drift slowly so the frame never freezes. Schematic; no molecular structures.
scenes.narration: How can you map a living human brain without opening the skull? Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, pictures brain structure. Functional MRI adds glowing patches during a task. What do those glowing patches measure?

scenes.visual: Title card 'Seeing Structure, Reading Blood' appears cleanly in large high-contrast type centered over the gently drifting brain-in-scanner silhouette.

scenes.tts: Structural M R I maps gray matter, white matter and lesions. Functional M R I reads blood instead, through hemoglobin's magnetism. Oxygen-poor hemoglobin, deoxyhemoglobin, disturbs the scanner's magnetic field; oxygen-rich hemoglobin barely does. Active regions receive more oxygenated blood than they use, so that disturbance shrinks. Seconds later, the blood oxygen level dependent, or BOLD, signal rises.

scenes.visual: In the same brain-in-scanner world, crisp anatomical boundaries highlight gray matter, white matter, and a dark lesion patch. A docked zoom window opens on the right showing a schematic cortical capillary beside active synapses: dark purple red-blood-cell discs labelled 'deoxyhemoglobin' ripple nearby magnetic field lines, while bright red discs labelled 'oxygen-rich hemoglobin' leave them smooth (schematic; no molecular structures). As the synapses flash, extra bright red discs rush through the capillary, the field ripples smooth out, and a docked schematic BOLD trace below rises after a few-second delay.

scenes.tts: Because BOLD reads blood, not neurons directly, which neural signal drives it? In 2001, Nikos Logothetis and colleagues recorded with electrodes inside a scanner in anaesthetized monkey visual cortex. At some sites under a long visual stimulus, synaptic currents stayed high while spiking fell near baseline. Predict: did BOLD stay high or drop?

At some sites under a long visual stimulus, synaptic currents stayed high while spiking fell near baseline. Predict: did BOLD stay high or drop?
scenes.visual: Same scanner ring, now holding a schematic monkey visual-cortex patch with a fine microelectrode lowered into it as a long visual stimulus bar turns on. Three stacked schematic traces draw left to right below: 'synaptic currents' stays on a high plateau; 'spiking' rises briefly then drops back near baseline; 'BOLD' starts to rise and pauses at a glowing question mark. High-contrast question card appears cleanly: 'Does BOLD stay high or drop?' Schematic.

In 2001, Nikos Logothetis and colleagues recorded with electrodes inside a scanner in anaesthetized monkey visual cortex. scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause: the question 'Does BOLD stay high or drop?' remains on screen while the schematic synaptic-current plateau and low spiking trace stay visible and two faint dotted candidate paths—one staying high, one dropping—pulse gently from the BOLD question mark. Schematic.

scenes.tts: BOLD stayed high, like the local field potential, the summed synaptic currents near the electrode. So BOLD seems to reflect input and local processing more than spiking output. The rule: M R I maps brain structure, while functional M R I reads delayed blood oxygenation. An active patch shows task involvement, not spikes or necessity.

scenes.visual: The schematic BOLD trace resolves solidly onto the high plateau, locking into step with the 'local field potential' trace while the 'spiking' trace stays low and dims. The cortical patch glows in the scanner ring, and three short high-contrast tags appear beside it: 'input and processing' checked, 'spiking output' dimmed, 'necessity' crossed out. Schematic.

scenes.tts: Three limits shape how we read scans. First, activation never shows a region is needed. Testing necessity still requires damage or silencing. Second, averaging scans across people can blur neighbouring regions into false overlap. Mapping regions inside each person first avoids that blur.

scenes.visual: Inside the scanner world, an active glow sits beside a 'lesion or silencing' badge: only the badge earns the word 'needed' (schematic). Then two schematic individual brains with slightly offset colour patches slide together into one blurred template where the patches falsely overlap, then pull apart into sharp person-by-person outlines labelled 'individual localizer'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: Three limits shape how we read scans. First, activation never shows a region is needed. Testing necessity still requires damage or silencing. Second, averaging scans across people can blur neighbouring regions into false overlap. Mapping regions inside each person first avoids that blur.

scenes.tts: Third, brain-wide links to behaviour across people are usually tiny. In 2022, Scott Marek and colleagues found a median association of zero point zero one. The median imaging study used about twenty-five people. Two such subsamples could support opposite conclusions. Replication improved only as samples reached thousands. Fix targets in advance, and test on people kept out of training.
scenes.caption: Third, brain-wide links to behaviour across people are usually tiny. In 2022, Scott Marek and colleagues found a median association of 0.01. The median imaging study used about 25 people. Two such subsamples could support opposite conclusions. Replication improved only as samples reached thousands. Fix targets in advance, and test on people kept out of training.
scenes.visual: Beside the scanner silhouette, a schematic scatter plot draws two small 25-point subsamples whose trend lines tilt in opposite directions, labelled 'n = 25'. Thousands of points then stream in ('3,928 participants'), collapsing the trend toward a near-flat slope labelled 'median 0.01' (schematic). A clean guard badge first pins a target marked 'chosen in advance', then splits whole people into 'train' and 'held-out people'. Schematic.

scenes.tts: With those guards, scans unlocked discoveries. In 2007, Nina Dronkers and colleagues scanned Paul Broca's two preserved 1861 brains with M R I. Both lesions reached deeper, into white matter, than Broca could measure from the surface. In 2011, Evelina Fedorenko and colleagues defined each person's language regions individually. Most responded little to arithmetic, working memory, or music.
scenes.caption: With those guards, scans unlocked discoveries. In 2007, Nina Dronkers and colleagues scanned Paul Broca's two preserved 1861 brains with MRI. scenes.visual: Returning to the brain inside the scanner ring, a structural slice of a preserved brain reveals a shaded lesion extending deep inward into white matter past a small surface mark, tagged 'Dronkers et al., 2007'. The view transitions smoothly to a living brain with crisp individually mapped language patches glowing for sentences while staying dim beside simple arithmetic and music icons, tagged 'Fedorenko et al., 2011'. Schematic.

scenes.tts: In 2012, Baliki, Apkarian and colleagues followed adults with recent back pain, not yet chronic, for a year. Stronger baseline connectivity, correlated activity between medial prefrontal cortex and nucleus accumbens, predicted persistence. The R O C area was zero point eight three.
scenes.caption: In 2012, Baliki, Apkarian and colleagues followed adults with recent back pain, not yet chronic, for a year. Stronger baseline connectivity, correlated activity between medial prefrontal cortex and nucleus accumbens, predicted persistence. The ROC area was 0.83.
scenes.visual: Inside the brain in the scanner ring, a glowing arc links medial prefrontal cortex and nucleus accumbens, pulsing in sync along a 1-year timeline tagged 'Baliki et al., 2012'. A tag 'ROC area 0.83' appears as it is spoken.

scenes.tts: That means in about eighty-three percent of random pairs, the persisting patient scored higher than the recovering one. Prediction is not cause. Read structure directly, and read every glow as delayed blood oxygenation, not spikes.
scenes.caption: That means in about 83% of random pairs, the persisting patient scored higher than the recovering one. Prediction is not cause. Read structure directly, and read every glow as delayed blood oxygenation, not spikes.
scenes.visual: Pairs of patient dots, one 'persisted' and one 'recovered', are drawn at random; in most pairs the persisting dot sits higher, and a counter settles near '83% of pairs' (schematic, illustrating the reported 0.83). A 'not cause' tag appears. For the final line, the arc fades into the clean dual picture of crisp structural brain outlines and the gently pulsing capillary blood signal beneath them. Schematic; no molecular structures.

scenes.visual: Clean high-contrast end card displaying only the take-home sentence 'MRI maps structure; fMRI reads blood oxygenation, not spikes or cause.' in large legible type over the softly dimming scanner-ring outline.
